variants.name: async/await with Task continuation state
variants.implementation_notes: Swift's concurrency absorbs the ACT: every suspension point becomes continuation state owned by the task, so the runtime resumes exactly that task when the awaited operation completes - the token is the task's own continuation, and Task.value/.result/cancel() are the client-side handles. Legacy callback APIs reappear as an explicit, checked token via withCheckedContinuation (see the bridge variant), and structured fan-out (withTaskGroup + addTask/next()/cancelAll()) demultiplexes completions of children created at run time. There is no registry to write; the residual work is ownership and cancellation.
pitfalls: Resuming a continuation more than once is undefined behaviour, and never resuming leaves the task suspended indefinitely and leaks its resources; CheckedContinuation detects misuse by logging/trapping, UnsafeContinuation does not.
Discarding a Task reference does not cancel it: you lose the ability to await or cancel that operation, and its completion is never demultiplexed.
Cancellation is cooperative: cancel()/cancelAll() only set a flag and a task group still waits for all children after an early return - poll Task.isCancelled/checkCancellation() in the operation.
A cancellation handler runs concurrently with the operation and may hold internal locks; completing a continuation from there risks double-resume or deadlock.

variants.name: CheckedContinuation bridge for callback APIs
variants.implementation_notes: Where the service still completes through a callback or a delegate, the continuation itself is the ACT: withCheckedContinuation creates it, the callback closure captures it, and resume(returning:)/resume(throwing:)/resume(with:) delivers the result to the suspended task. The task keeps its own state, so no client-side table is needed, but the exactly-once rule is now yours, and a callback that may never fire needs an explicit timeout path. UnsafeContinuation is the same object without the runtime's misuse checks - justify it by measurement, not by convenience.
pitfalls: A callback that can fire twice (retry, duplicate notification) double-resumes the continuation: guard with a flag or an actor-held state, because with UnsafeContinuation the mistake is silent.
Never-resolving callbacks hang the task forever - pair the bridge with a timeout and resume with a failure on expiry.
